subsection: 2. O'Neill and the Civil Rights movement, 1963–1969

notes.h: Background: a divided state and the grievances of the Catholic minority
notes.b: To understand why a civil rights movement appeared in the 1960s, you need to know how Northern Ireland was run and what Catholics complained about. The background and key ideas used throughout the topic come first.
points: Northern Ireland was created by the Government of Ireland Act (1920) and came into operation in 1921. The Ulster Unionist Party governed at Stormont (the Northern Ireland parliament) continuously from 1921 to 1972, so the state was Protestant and unionist in character.

Catholics were about one third of the population (about 35 per cent in the 1961 census) and were mostly nationalists, who wanted a united Ireland. This meant they were a permanent minority who could never win a majority at Stormont.

In local elections only ratepayers (householders) and their spouses could vote, and companies had extra votes. In Westminster elections all adults could vote. This is why 'one man, one vote' (every adult having one vote) was a demand about local elections only.

Gerrymandering means drawing electoral boundaries to give one group an advantage. In Derry nationalists were a clear majority of the population, but unionists controlled Londonderry Corporation (the city council) because of the way the ward boundaries were drawn.

Unionist-controlled councils allocated council houses and many local jobs, so Catholics complained of discrimination in housing and employment. They also resented the Special Powers Act (1922, giving the government sweeping emergency powers), the B Specials (the part-time Ulster Special Constabulary) and the RUC (the police).

Brookeborough was Prime Minister from 1943 to 1963 and left these grievances in place, so they were waiting for O'Neill. The welfare state had also produced a more educated Catholic middle class, less willing to accept them. There is more on this in the notes on Brookeborough's Northern Ireland.

Civil rights means equal treatment of Catholics in voting, housing and jobs, sought by peaceful protest and by appeals to British opinion. Tolerance is willingness to accept other beliefs and identities; intolerance is refusing to.
The unionist and nationalist divide, and Paisley's opposition to reform, are the examples of intolerance used in this topic, because each side often refused to accept the other's identity.
notes.tip: Define gerrymandering and civil rights briefly and use Derry as your example. Remember that the franchise demand applied to local elections only, because Westminster already had a universal vote.

notes.b: Terence O'Neill came to power in 1963 believing that Northern Ireland's future lay in a modern, prosperous economy. His programme combined economic planning with gestures towards Catholics.
points: Terence O'Neill succeeded Lord Brookeborough as Prime Minister in March 1963, having been Minister of Finance from 1956. His time at Finance gave him the experience of economic planning that shaped his premiership.

The Matthew Report (the Belfast Regional Survey and Plan, 1963, by Sir Robert Matthew) was a plan for regional development around Belfast. It proposed a new city, and Craigavon in County Armagh (Lurgan and Portadown) was planned from these proposals, with government acceptance in 1964.

The Wilson Plan (Economic Development in Northern Ireland, 1965, by Professor Thomas Wilson) was about economic development generally, not about the new city. Together the two reports shaped planning, so it is wrong to credit Craigavon to the Wilson Plan alone.

Government-backed projects such as Craigavon and the new university at Coleraine were part of a wider plan to show that Northern Ireland could be modern and prosperous. Coleraine's choice as the site angered Derry, which had wanted the university.

O'Neill made symbolic visits to Catholic schools and hospitals. This was a famous gesture of goodwill towards a community that had been shut out of public life, and unionist hardliners resented it as a concession to nationalists, because it suggested that the government might treat them as equal citizens.
notes.tip: Do not say the Wilson Plan led to Craigavon. Say the Matthew Report and the Wilson Plan both shaped planning, with Craigavon coming from the Matthew proposals. Do not confuse Thomas Wilson the economist with Harold Wilson the British Prime Minister.

notes.b: O'Neill went beyond economics and tried to improve relations with Catholics and with the Republic of Ireland. This policy is known as bridge-building, and its high point was the exchange of visits with the Taoiseach in 1965.
points: Bridge-building was O'Neill's name for his policy of improving relations with Catholics in Northern Ireland and with the government of the Republic. He hoped that prosperity and goodwill would reduce the tension between the two communities.

On 14 January 1965 the Taoiseach, Seán Lemass, visited Stormont. This meeting is often described as the first between the heads of the two governments since partition, though earlier contacts existed in the early 1920s, so the phrase should not be given as flat fact.
O'Neill returned the visit to Dublin on 9 February 1965. He had not told most of his cabinet in advance, which shows that he expected opposition within his own government.

Nationalists responded in February 1965 when the Nationalist Party, led by Eddie McAteer, became the official opposition at Stormont for the first time. This was a sign that some nationalists were prepared to work within the state, which shows that some nationalists were prepared to work within the state.

Catholics welcomed the gestures but judged that real change in housing, jobs and voting was too slow. Visits and speeches had not altered the council allocation of houses or the local franchise, so hopes were raised without being met.
notes.tip: Write 'often described as' for the Lemass meeting. In essays on how successful O'Neill was, use the Lemass meeting and the Catholic reaction to show both what he achieved and why it was not enough.

notes.b: O'Neill's reforms split his own side. Hardline unionists saw the Lemass meeting as the first step towards a united Ireland, and they began to organise against him.
points: Ian Paisley, a Protestant minister, was by the mid-1960s the leading Protestant critic of O'Neill's policies. He and other hardliners opposed the Lemass meeting, arguing that it undermined the Union (the link with Britain) and Protestant identity.

The 'O'Neill must go' campaign, led by Paisley and others from 1966, sought the Prime Minister's removal from office. Its rallies showed O'Neill that a section of the unionist community would not accept his policy of bridge-building, because it showed that part of the unionist community would not accept bridge-building.

In 1966 Paisley set up the Ulster Constitution Defence Committee and the Ulster Protestant Volunteers. He was jailed for three months in 1966 after a June protest at the Presbyterian General Assembly in Belfast, when he refused to be bound over (to promise to keep the peace).

William Craig, Minister of Home Affairs from 1966, was a hardline figure in the cabinet who banned the Derry march of 5 October 1968. O'Neill dismissed him on 11 December 1968 after he clashed with O'Neill over policy.

Unionist MPs in the Stormont parliament and in the party organisation argued that O'Neill was giving away too much to nationalists. Opposition therefore came from inside the Unionist Party, not just from street protest.

The Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), a loyalist paramilitary group, murdered three people in May and June 1966: John Scullion, Peter Ward (a Catholic barman) and Matilda Gould. Its leader Gusty Spence was convicted of the murder of Ward and jailed for life. This was the violent edge of loyalism.

O'Neill was therefore squeezed between reformers, who thought he was too slow, and hardliners, who thought he was going too fast. His position weakened as unionist opposition grew and as violence on both sides increased in 1968 and 1969.
notes.tip: Do not give William Craig's dismissal a single cause such as a unilateral declaration of independence. Say he was dismissed in December 1968 after clashing with O'Neill over policy. Do not confuse him with James Craig or with the city of Craigavon.

notes.b: O'Neill was the reforming Prime Minister whose policies helped to create the conditions for the civil rights movement, and whose authority collapsed under its pressure. Examiners want a verdict on him, not a biography.
points: He was born in London on 10 September 1914 into a landed family whose seat was Shane's Castle, County Antrim, and he was educated at Eton. He entered Stormont in 1946, was Minister of Finance from 1956 to 1963 and became Prime Minister in 1963.

As Prime Minister he made modernisation and reconciliation the centre of his programme, because he believed prosperity would ease sectarian tension. He drew on the Matthew and Wilson reports and tried to build contact with Dublin through the Lemass meetings of 1965.
In 1968 and 1969 he came under pressure from London, from the civil rights movement and from within his own party, so he conceded reforms step by step.
He announced the five-point package on 22 November 1968 and appealed for moderation in the 'Ulster stands at the crossroads' broadcast on 9 December 1968.
As Prime Minister he was a participant who decided policy and spoke for the government; later he wrote and gave interviews about the crisis as a witness.

He resigned on 28 April 1969 after a crisis in his party, a poor showing in the February election and a series of bomb attacks on water and electricity installations. He was made a life peer in 1970 as Baron O'Neill of the Maine, and died in 1990.
Contemporaries were divided. Hardline unionists accused him of betraying the Union, nationalists welcomed the gestures but judged them too slow, and British opinion backed him.

Historians generally judge him a modernising planner and a sincere but limited reformer, who reformed on his own terms and from above. Some argue that he did not regard Catholic grievances as primarily political, citing his reported 1969 opinion that Catholics given jobs and houses would live like Protestants.
Historians also note that his authority was constrained by his own party, which is why they debate whether he was a failure or a reformer who was undermined.
notes.tip: Examiners ask how successful O'Neill was, often against Brookeborough or Paisley. State a clear judgement early and support it with dated points on both sides: planning, the Lemass meeting and the five points against failing to reform in time, hold his party or prevent violence. Separate his intentions from what he achieved.

notes.h: Key personality: Conn and Patricia McCluskey
notes.b: Dr Conn McCluskey and his wife Patricia gathered evidence of discrimination against Catholics through the Campaign for Social Justice. Their moderate, documentary campaign made discrimination a public issue before the mass movement began.
points: Conn McCluskey was a Dungannon doctor and Patricia was his wife. In 1963 Patricia and others set up the Dungannon Homeless Citizens League, which campaigned about the allocation of council houses in the town.

The league grew into the Campaign for Social Justice in Northern Ireland, founded in January 1964 in Dungannon, County Tyrone. It gathered evidence on discrimination in housing, jobs and local government in Tyrone, Fermanagh and Derry, and published it in pamphlets such as 'Northern Ireland: the Plain Truth'.

The McCluskeys were participants who led the campaign. They sent their findings to MPs at Westminster, and the lobbying helped to lead to the formation of the Campaign for Democracy in Ulster at Westminster in 1965, made up of Labour MPs and others such as Paul Rose.

They shaped events by providing evidence and a model of constitutional protest, and they were ahead of NICRA (the Civil Rights Association). Their method was documentary and moderate, appealing to British opinion through facts rather than street protest, because it gave the movement a model to follow.

Some unionists dismissed the campaign as a front for republicans, a charge the McCluskeys rejected; they described their aim as equal treatment of citizens. Nationalists and sympathetic British MPs welcomed the evidence.

Historians credit the Campaign for Social Justice with turning discrimination into a public issue before the Civil Rights Association was formed, so its work provided the evidence on which the later movement drew.
notes.tip: For an Ordinary Level paragraph, give the dates: 1963 for the Homeless Citizens League and January 1964 for the Campaign for Social Justice. Do not confuse the Campaign for Social Justice (1964) with NICRA (1967), the Campaign for Democracy in Ulster (1965) or People's Democracy (1968).

notes.h: Why the movement emerged, and the Civil Rights Association and its demands
notes.b: By the mid-1960s several developments came together to make a mass civil rights movement possible. The Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association (NICRA) was founded in 1967 to campaign for equal rights for Catholics on the British model.
points: The movement emerged now for several reasons. There was a generation of educated Catholics produced by the welfare state, the American civil rights movement of the 1960s offered an example of peaceful protest, and a Labour government under Harold Wilson came to power in Britain in 1964.

O'Neill's gestures had also raised Catholic hopes without delivering change, and the McCluskeys' evidence gave campaigners facts to use. In short, expectations had risen faster than reform, because new hopes had been created without matching reforms.

NICRA was founded in Belfast on 29 January 1967. It drew together the Campaign for Social Justice, nationalists, republicans, socialists, trade unionists, Communists, Labour supporters and some liberal Protestants.

Its demands were one man, one vote in local elections, an end to gerrymandering, fair allocation of council houses on a points system and laws against discrimination by public bodies. It also demanded the repeal of the Special Powers Act and the disbanding of the B Specials.

Westminster elections already used one man, one vote, so the demand applied to local elections, where the franchise was restricted to ratepayers and their spouses and companies had a vote. This is why it was the central and most contested demand.
The movement used peaceful marches and sit-ins to draw attention to discrimination, and it sought British support for reform, so peaceful pressure was the movement's chosen method.
notes.tip: Essays ask why the movement emerged and how far it succeeded, and both halves matter. For causes, link discrimination in housing, jobs and voting to the educated Catholic generation, the McCluskeys, the American example and O'Neill's raised expectations.

notes.h: From Caledon to Armagh: the first protests, 1968
notes.b: In 1968 the movement moved from complaint to action. A series of dated protests, easily confused with one another, shows how it grew and how the authorities and loyalists reacted.
points: On 20 June 1968 at Caledon, County Tyrone, Austin Currie, a Nationalist MP at Stormont, squatted in a council house that had been allocated to a single 19-year-old Protestant secretary. He was evicted by the RUC, and the incident drew attention to housing allocation.

NICRA's first march, from Coalisland to Dungannon on 24 August 1968, was followed by marches in Derry, Newry and Belfast. It showed that the movement could draw a crowd and keep the protest peaceful, so it proved that the movement could draw a crowd and keep order.

The authorities banned or obstructed many marches, which led to confrontations with the police and loyalist counter-demonstrators. Bans turned peaceful protest into a test of whether the state would allow it.

On 30 November 1968 a NICRA march in Armagh was blocked by Paisley's followers and others. This shows how counter-demonstrations were used to stop marches, and it was a confrontation between supporters of Paisley and the movement.
notes.tip: Learn the sequence: Caledon (June 1968, squatting), Coalisland to Dungannon (24 August, the first march), Derry (5 October, banned), Armagh (30 November, blocked), Burntollet (4 January 1969). A common mistake is calling Burntollet a NICRA march.

notes.b: The banned civil rights march in Derry was broken up by the police. Television pictures of the violence turned the movement into an international story.
points: Derry was a flashpoint because it had a Catholic majority but unionist control of Londonderry Corporation through gerrymandering. Housing and jobs were also scarce, and many Catholics felt neglected.

The march of 5 October 1968 was organised by NICRA and was banned by the Minister of Home Affairs, William Craig. Marchers who defied the ban were confronted by RUC officers, who used batons on the crowd in Duke Street.
Gerry Fitt, MP for Belfast West at Westminster, was among those struck. Film shot by RTÉ and others was seen widely and shocked opinion in Britain and Ireland.

The event is seen as the start of the civil rights crisis of 1968 and 1969, because it moved the movement from marches to confrontation. Riots followed in Derry, and British and international attention increased, because the violence showed that the demand for change was being met by force.
Nationalists in Derry saw the police action as proof of discrimination, while unionists blamed the civil rights organisers for provoking disorder.
The Derry Citizens' Action Committee was formed in October 1968, with John Hume as vice-chairman, to keep protests peaceful. At the same time, students were radicalised by what they saw.
notes.tip: Do not confuse 5 October 1968 (RUC batons, Duke Street, banned by Craig) with the Battle of the Bogside of August 1969 or with Bloody Sunday in 1972. Only the first belongs to this topic.

notes.h: O'Neill's response: British pressure, the five points and the broadcast
notes.b: After Derry, the British government pressed O'Neill to act. His response was a package of reforms that went some way towards the civil rights demands but left the central one untouched.
points: British pressure was direct. Harold Wilson, the British Prime Minister, met O'Neill, Craig and Faulkner in London on 4 November 1968.
The five-point package of 22 November 1968 promised a points system for allocating council houses, so that need rather than religion would decide who got a house.

It promised an ombudsman, a Parliamentary Commissioner, to investigate complaints against government departments, and it promised that Londonderry Corporation would be replaced by a development commission.
It promised that the Special Powers Act would be withdrawn when the situation allowed, and that the company vote in local elections would be ended.
One man, one vote in local elections was not in the package, which was the main demand of the movement. The parliamentary party accepted it only in April 1969.

On 9 December 1968 O'Neill made his 'Ulster stands at the crossroads' television broadcast, appealing for moderation. Many moderates backed him and hardliners were angry; Craig was dismissed two days later, on 11 December.
notes.tip: Never say the five points included one man, one vote. List the five points with their reforms, then say that the main demand was not conceded. This is the commonest mistake in answers on the package.

notes.b: Some young activists thought NICRA's methods were too cautious. People's Democracy, a student group, marched across Northern Ireland, and the attack on its march made the crisis worse.
points: People's Democracy was formed on 9 October 1968 at Queen's University Belfast, after the Derry march, by students including Bernadette Devlin and Michael Farrell. Its aim was to press for civil rights and for one man, one vote, because some students thought NICRA too cautious.

The march from Belfast to Derry began on 1 January 1969, with about 40 people at the start. The aim was to protest against discrimination and to press for one man, one vote, in the manner of American civil rights marches.
On 4 January 1969 the marchers were ambushed at Burntollet Bridge, near Derry, by loyalists, among whom were off-duty B Specials. The RUC failed to protect the march.

On the night of 4-5 January RUC men went through the Catholic Bogside, and residents set up barricades. 'Free Derry' became the name for the area, after the slogan painted on a gable end in January 1969.

The effect was a loss of Catholic confidence in the RUC, because marchers and supporters accused it of failing to protect the march. The movement became more confrontational, and in early 1969 NICRA and People's Democracy briefly split over tactics.
notes.tip: Burntollet was a People's Democracy march, not a NICRA march. Use 'about 40 at the start' for the marchers and give no figure for those attacked or injured.

notes.h: The crisis of 1969 and O'Neill's resignation
notes.b: Through the spring of 1969 O'Neill lost control of his party. A divided election, a wave of bombs and the demand for one man, one vote ended his premiership.
points: The Stormont general election on 24 February 1969 left the Unionist Party divided between pro-O'Neill and anti-O'Neill candidates, and its overall result was disappointing for O'Neill, which showed that his party was split down the middle.
O'Neill held his own seat at Bannside against Paisley by a majority of 1,414 votes. A narrow win against a hardline challenger showed how far his support among unionists had fallen.

Bombs at water and electricity installations, including the Silent Valley reservoir in the Mournes, began on 30 March 1969. They were first blamed on the IRA but were later shown to be the work of loyalists in the UVF, who hoped to discredit O'Neill, and they undermined his position.
The Mid Ulster by-election on 17 April 1969 returned Bernadette Devlin as a unity candidate. Do not confuse it with the general election of 24 February.
In April 1969 the cabinet debated one man, one vote, and the Unionist parliamentary party accepted it in local elections. This split the party further, because hardliners saw it as surrender.

O'Neill resigned on 28 April 1969. James Chichester-Clark became Prime Minister by 17 votes to 16 over Brian Faulkner, a one-vote margin. The crisis led on to the Troubles; there is more on this in the notes on the outbreak of the Troubles.
notes.tip: Keep the two 1969 contests apart: the Stormont general election (24 February, O'Neill holds Bannside) and the Mid Ulster by-election (17 April, Devlin elected). Do not say the parliamentary party accepted one man, one vote without noting the cabinet had debated it first.

notes.b: Devlin was a student leader and civil rights activist who, in 1969, became the youngest woman elected to Westminster at the time. She carried the movement's demands into the British parliament.
points: Bernadette Devlin was born on 23 April 1947 in Cookstown, County Tyrone, and studied psychology at Queen's University Belfast, where she became a leading student activist, so she was a student leader before she was an MP.
She was a participant in People's Democracy, formed in October 1968, and in the Belfast to Derry march of January 1969. She became a prominent speaker in the civil rights campaign.
She was elected MP for Mid Ulster at the by-election of 17 April 1969, aged twenty-one, as a unity candidate. She was the youngest woman elected to Westminster up to then.

She shaped events by carrying civil rights to Westminster, and was in turn shaped by the movement that made her a public figure. She wrote a memoir, The Price of My Soul, published in 1969, which presented the struggle from her own perspective.
Contemporary nationalists and supporters saw her as a symbol of youth and defiance, while unionists regarded her as a dangerous agitator.
Historians tend to view her as a key figure who brought the civil rights movement into Westminster politics.

She was convicted of incitement to riot after the Battle of the Bogside in August 1969 and served a sentence in 1970. On 31 January 1972, after Bloody Sunday, she struck the Home Secretary Reginald Maudling in the House of Commons.
She lost her Westminster seat in February 1974, and in January 1981 she and her husband were seriously wounded by loyalist gunmen at their home.
notes.tip: For a personality paragraph give dates and deeds: birth year 1947, People's Democracy, Burntollet in January 1969 and the April 1969 election. In essays on pairs of personalities, give her a sphere of influence and a clear verdict.

notes.b: Paisley's opposition to O'Neill made him the most visible unionist critic of reform before 1969. His career is covered here to 1969 only.
points: Ian Paisley was born in 1926 in Armagh and was a minister who founded the Free Presbyterian Church of Ulster in 1951. Its doctrine was strict, anti-Catholic and anti-ecumenical (opposed to friendly contact between Churches). Do not confuse it with the Presbyterian Church in Ireland.

Before 1969 he was a public campaigner who organised rallies and protests against O'Neill's policies. He founded the Protestant Telegraph in 1966, set up the Ulster Constitution Defence Committee and the Ulster Protestant Volunteers, and was jailed for three months in 1966.

He opposed the Lemass meeting, arguing that the Prime Minister was undermining the Union and Protestant identity, and he led the 'O'Neill must go' campaign. His followers helped to block the NICRA march in Armagh on 30 November 1968.
He was a participant in his own campaign and, through his followers, in the Armagh blocking and the Bannside contest of February 1969, where O'Neill held the seat against him by a majority of 1,414.

He shaped events by mobilising grassroots Protestant opinion and restricting O'Neill's room to reform; his stand grew with each concession, which is why the more he conceded, the harder the hardliners pushed.

Contemporaries saw him as the voice of hardline unionism: many unionists regarded him as a defender of the Union and Protestant identity, moderates found him an embarrassment, and nationalists saw him as a bigot.

Historians argue that his campaign against O'Neill helped to pull unionist politics towards the harder line of the 1970s. In April 1970 he won the Bannside seat at Stormont at a by-election after O'Neill's departure.
notes.tip: Essays on Paisley and O'Neill need a sphere of influence and a clear verdict for each, not a biography. Give each a date and a deed, such as the 1966 jail sentence and the Armagh blocking of 30 November 1968.

notes.h: Assessment: O'Neill and the civil rights movement
notes.b: Judging this period means weighing what reform achieved against what it failed to do, and separating aims from results. The points below are paired to help you build a balanced argument.
points: O'Neill's successes: he modernised the economy through planning and Craigavon, built bridges to Catholics and Dublin, and conceded much of the civil rights programme, including a points system for housing, an ombudsman and, by April 1969, one man, one vote in local elections.

O'Neill's limits: his reforms came late, after the Derry march of October 1968 and British pressure, and he did not tackle discrimination until forced. They were too slow for Catholics and the movement but too fast for his party, so he lost control.

The movement's successes: it put discrimination on the British political agenda, brought the question of Northern Ireland's government into the open and secured reforms such as the points system, the ombudsman and one man, one vote.

The movement's limits: it provoked a loyalist reaction, bans and violence, and some of its leaders were divided, as in the split between NICRA and People's Democracy. Many leaders judged the reforms concessions forced by protest.
Contemporary views: nationalists welcomed the gains but argued that discrimination had not ended. Unionists were divided, with hardliners blaming the movement for provoking violence.

Later views: Michael Farrell stresses systematic discrimination by the unionist state, Marc Mulholland sees a reformer constrained by his party, and Thomas Hennessey examines the O'Neill years and the build-up to violence.
Overall, reform from above met resistance from below and a unionist backlash, and his resignation in April 1969 showed the limits of reform from above. The crisis led to the Troubles.
notes.tip: Better answers separate the aims of the movement from its results and separate O'Neill's intentions from what he achieved. Use evidence from hardline unionists and nationalists rather than telling the story.

The drawing of electoral boundaries to give one group an advantage, which the civil rights movement targeted in local government in Derry and elsewhere.
Tolerance is willingness to accept differing beliefs and identities, while intolerance is refusal to accept them, a key divide between unionists and nationalists in this period.
O'Neill's policy of improving relations with Catholics and with the Republic of Ireland through gestures and meetings.
The Northern Ireland Civil Rights Association, founded in 1967 to campaign for equal rights for Catholics.

O'Neill's reforms of 22 November 1968: a points system for housing, an ombudsman, replacement of Londonderry Corporation by a commission, withdrawal of the Special Powers Act when possible, and an end to the company vote.
A student-led civil rights organisation formed at Queen's University Belfast in October 1968, which organised the Belfast to Derry march.
The ambush on 4 January 1969 by loyalists at Burntollet Bridge on the People's Democracy march to Derry.
The church Ian Paisley founded in 1951, which combined strict Protestant doctrine with opposition to ecumenism and to concessions to nationalists.
The demand for a single vote for each adult in local elections, replacing the ratepayer franchise and company votes; accepted by O'Neill's party in April 1969.
The body founded by Conn and Patricia McCluskey in 1964 to collect evidence of discrimination and publicise it at Westminster.
